title: Dead Air / CBR + PNK / Games that nail their A E S T H E T I C S
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jTEvYjhQKTM

Daniel (@dungeondive) admits he hasn't played either game here. This is purely a look at two indie releases whose visual design does half the work. The first is Dead Air, designed by Fiona of Sleepy Sparrow Games and published by Anna Blackwell (of Delve). You run a radio station in post-nuclear Scotland and record your broadcasts as audio journals. The zine alternates trustworthy out-of-character rules pages with in-character found documents: cigarette-burned maps, hand-scrawled lookup tables, transmitter schematics and an advert for the FW-390. The Kickstarter extras go further, with a microphone-technique pamphlet, a duck-and-cover postcard, a takeaway menu from the Black Lagoon, and a letter granting his station a ten-week broadcast licence that thanks him for volunteering.

The second is CBR+PNK, a streamlined Forged in the Dark game for one-last-run cyberpunk one-shots, which he bought purely as a package. A slipcase holds a fold-out rules pamphlet and dry-erase character sheets. Supplements cover the weird (Shadowrun-style magic), a lunar Predator-meets-Aliens setting, a three-act monorail heist, cyber-Hunters, and Mona Rise, a setting for William Gibson's Sprawl. He rolls up a sample job live: smuggling a celebrity out through the docks during a nightclub power outage. He suggests the run-builder could support solo play, and wishes every panel had a lookup table.

Both games put form over function, with tiny tables and scattered rules that make them harder to learn. He doesn't mind. For him, as a book collector, the artistic design can be as rewarding as playing.

----

Daniel bought CBR+PNK for its design alone. Have you ever bought a game purely as a beautiful object, and did you end up playing it?
